stem:
A 32-year-old contact lens wearer presents with severe eye pain, ring-shaped stromal infiltrate, and radial keratoneuritis.
Trophozoites and double-walled cysts are suspected. What is the specific staining method used for definitive laboratory
identification of this pathogen?
rationale:
Acanthamoeba cysts fluoresce bright green under UV light when stained with Calcofluor white, and Giemsa highlights
trophozoites. Culturing requires non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli.

stem:
In a patient with advanced keratoconus undergoing Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK), which anatomical layers
are completely retained in the recipient bed?
rationale:
Acanthamoeba cysts fluoresce bright green under UV light when stained with Calcofluor white, and Giemsa highlights
trophozoites. Culturing requires non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli.

stem:
A 40-year-old male with chronic recurrent corneal erosions is diagnosed with Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy. Which
specific corneal layer is primarily affected and replaced by cellular connective tissue?
rationale:
Reis-Bücklers dystrophy is an autosomal dominant anterior corneal dystrophy characterized by destruction and replacement of
Bowman's layer with sheet-like collagen filaments (TGFBI gene mutation).

stem:
A patient with neurotrophic keratopathy secondary to acoustic neuroma resection exhibits complete corneal anesthesia
and a persistent epithelial defect (Stage 2). What is the primary pathophysiological driver of neurotrophic corneal breakdown?

options.A: Excessive lacrimal gland hypersecretion driven by CN VII
options.B: Immune complex deposition in Descemet's membrane
options.C: Primary vascular endothelial ischemia of limbal palisades
options.D: Overproduction of matrix metalloproteinases by conjunctival goblet cells
options.E: Loss of sensory trophic factors (e.g., Substance P, NGF) supplied by CN V1

rationale:
Trigeminal nerve (CN V1) damage leads to loss of corneal sensation and sensory neuromodulators (NGF, Substance P,
CGRP), impairing epithelial mitosis, metabolic maintenance, and reflex blinking.

stem:
During specular microscopy of the corneal endothelium, a 65-year-old patient displays significant polymegathism and
pleomorphism. What physiological parameters do these terms represent?

options.A: Increased guttae count & Stromal hydration ratio
options.B: Variation in endothelial cell area (CV) & Variation in hexagonal cell shape (% hexagonality)
options.C: Decreased cell density & Increased central corneal thickness
options.D: Loss of Descemet's membrane thickness & Hypertrophy of stroma
options.E: Endothelial cell death rate & Mitotic index

rationale:
Polymegathism refers to variation in endothelial cell size (Coefficient of Variation, CV >0.40), while pleomorphism refers to loss
of normal hexagonal cell shape (% hexagonality <60%).

stem:
In Terrien's marginal degeneration, what is the characteristic anatomical location and clinical presentation of corneal
thinning?

options.A: 360-degree circumferential ulceration with steep overhangs and severe pain
options.B: Nasal interpalpebral epithelial breakdown with calcification
options.C: Superior peripheral non-ulcerative guttering with vascularization and lipid deposition
options.D: Central conical ectasia with Fleischer ring
options.E: Inferior peripheral thinning with lipid deposition and painful ulceration

rationale:
Terrien's marginal degeneration is a non-inflammatory, painless bilateral condition characterized by superior peripheral corneal
guttering, pannus, and lipid line deposition, causing against-the-rule astigmatism.

stem:
Mooren's ulcer is a severe idiopathic peripheral ulcerative keratitis. What key clinical feature distinguishes Mooren's ulcer
from systemic vasculitis-associated corneal melting (e.g., GPA or RA)?

options.A: Unilateral presentation always in elderly patients
options.B: High response to topical antibiotics alone

rationale:
Mooren's ulcer is strictly limited to the cornea and NEVER involves the adjacent sclera. Scleral involvement (scleritis) strongly
indicates an underlying systemic autoimmune disease (e.g., RA, GPA, SLE).

stem:
A neonate presents with bilateral cloudy corneas at birth. Intraocular pressure is normal, corneal diameter is normal, but
histological examination reveals absence of Descemet's membrane and endothelium centrally with posterior stromal defect
and iridocorneal adhesions. What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Peters anomaly is an inborn anterior segment dysgeneses featuring central absence of Descemet's membrane and
endothelium with posterior stromal opacity and keratolenticular or iridocorneal adhesions.

stem: What is the gold standard diagnostic test to confirm limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD)?

options.E: Impression cytology demonstrating conjunctival goblet cells on the cornea

rationale:
Impression cytology showing goblet cells and cytokeratin-13/19 expression on the corneal surface confirms conjunctivalization,
the hallmark of Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency.

stem:
In a patient with corneal graft rejection following penetrating keratoplasty (PKP), what is the specific named endothelial
rejection line composed of inflammatory cells called?
rationale:
The Khodadoust line is an endothelial rejection line consisting of lymphocytes and neutrophils advancing across the donor
cornea, marking active endothelial graft rejection.

stem:
A 58-year-old diabetic female presents with bilateral corneal opacity. Slit lamp reveals greyish-white, elevated, nodular
epithelial/subepithelial lesions in the interpalpebral zone. Histology shows hyaline material. What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Salzmann nodular degeneration features bluish-white or grey subepithelial fibrous nodules, typically developing secondary to
chronic ocular surface inflammation (blepharitis, dry eye, phlyctenulosis).

stem:
What is the primary mechanism of action of Netarsudil, a modern Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitor, when used in corneal
endothelial disease or glaucoma?

options.A: Decreases aqueous production via alpha-2 agonism
options.B: Increases uveoscleral outflow via FP receptor stimulation
options.C: Enhances trabecular meshwork outflow & promotes endothelial cell adhesion/proliferation
options.D: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase II in ciliary epithelium
options.E: Causes osmotic shift out of the vitreous

rationale:
ROCK inhibitors lower IOP by relaxing trabecular meshwork cells and reducing episcleral venous pressure, while also
promoting corneal endothelial cell survival and migration.

stem: In Band Keratopathy, calcium hydroxyapatite crystals deposit primarily in which corneal layer?
rationale:
Calcific band keratopathy involves calcium phosphate/hydroxyapatite deposition in the epithelial basement membrane,
Bowman's layer, and superficial anterior stroma within the interpalpebral fissure.

stem: What is the definitive treatment to clear calcific band keratopathy when visual acuity is threatened?

options.C: Chelation with topical EDTA (Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) after epithelial debridement

rationale:
Epithelial scraping followed by application of 1.5% to 3% disodium EDTA chelation binds and dissolves calcium hydroxyapatite
deposits.

stem:
A patient with systemic rheumatoid arthritis develops severe peripheral corneal melting with perforation (keratolysis).
What is the underlying enzymatic mechanism driving matrix breakdown?

options.A: Upregulation of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-8 and MMP-9) by neutrophils and keratocytes
options.B: Hypersecretion of lysozyme by lacrimal glands
options.D: Inhibition of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMP-1)
options.E: Immune complex activation of Na+/K+-ATPase pump

rationale:
Autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is driven by immune complex deposition at the limbus, recruiting neutrophils
that release MMP-8 (collagenase) and MMP-9, destroying stromal collagen.

stem: What is the diagnostic significance of a positive Seidel test during corneal examination?

options.B: Detects intraocular pressure elevation above 40 mmHg
options.E: Demonstrates aqueous humor leakage through a full-thickness corneal wound or perforation

rationale:
Concentrated 2% fluorescein instilled over a suspected wound dilutes and streams downward as clear aqueous humor leaks
out, demonstrating a positive Seidel test for full-thickness wound leakage.

stem:
In a patient with Marfan syndrome vs. Homocystinuria, what are the characteristic directions of lens subluxation (ectopia
lentis) respectively?

options.A: Downward & Nasal in Marfan; Upward & Temporal in Homocystinuria
options.B: Upward & Temporal in Marfan; Downward & Nasal in Homocystinuria
options.D: Directly Anterior into AC in Marfan; Posterior into Vitreous in Homocystinuria

rationale:
Marfan syndrome (Fibrillin-1 defect) causes superior-temporal lens dislocation with intact zonules; Homocystinuria
(cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) causes inferior-nasal dislocation with zonular disintegration.

stem: What is the fundamental pathological distinction between Phacolytic Glaucoma and Phacomorphic Glaucoma?

options.A:
Phacolytic is open-angle caused by trabecular meshwork clogging by high-MW lens proteins from hypermature cataract;
Phacomorphic is secondary angle-closure from an intumescent swollen lens
options.B: Phacolytic is angle-closure; Phacomorphic is open-angle
options.C: Phacolytic requires vitrectomy; Phacomorphic requires corneal transplant
options.D: Phacolytic occurs after trauma; Phacomorphic occurs only in neonates
options.E: Phacolytic is autoimmune response to intact capsule; Phacomorphic is genetic

rationale:
Phacolytic glaucoma = open-angle glaucoma where high molecular weight lens proteins leak through an intact microscopic
capsule in hypermature cataract, ingested by macrophages that clog trabecular meshwork. Phacomorphic = secondary angle closure from
intumescent lens mass.

stem:
In calculating IOL power using third-generation formulas (e.g., Hoffer Q, Holladay 1, SRK/T), which optical measurement
determines formula selection for short axial lengths (<22.0 mm)?

options.A: Flatter K values dictate using Haigis formula only
options.B: Hoffer Q is most accurate for short axial lengths (<22.0 mm)
options.C: SRK/T is preferred for short eyes
options.D: Holladay 2 is exclusively used for long eyes (>26.0 mm)
options.E: All formulas give identical calculations regardless of axial length

rationale:
Hoffer Q is proven most accurate for short axial lengths (<22.0 mm); SRK/T is best for long eyes (>26.0 mm); Holladay 1 and
Barrett Universal II perform well across average lengths.

stem:
What is the main cause of 'Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome' (TASS) occurring within 12–24 hours
post-phacoemulsification?

options.A: Retained lens fragment in posterior segment
options.D: Non-infectious inflammatory reaction to chemical contaminants, autoclaving residue, or balanced salt solution impurities
options.E: Bacterial endophthalmitis due to Staph epidermidis

rationale:
TASS is a sterile, acute anterior segment inflammation developing within 12-24 hours postoperatively caused by toxic
chemical residues on surgical instruments, denatured viscoelastic, or BSS additives.

stem:
A patient presents with 'Posterior Polar Cataract'. During phacoemulsification, what specific intraoperative complication
must the surgeon be extraordinarily prepared for?

options.D: Pre-existing tear or extreme fragility of the central posterior capsule

rationale:
Posterior polar cataracts are directly adherent to or involve dysplasia of the central posterior capsule. Capsular rupture occurs
in up to 20-30% of cases during hydrodissection or nucleus rotation.

stem:
In Phacoemulsification, what physical phenomenon causes cavitation and nuclear emulsification at the tip of the
ultrasound handpiece?

options.B: Electrical discharge between tip and sleeve
options.C: High-pressure irrigation stream splitting lens fibers
options.E: Rapid forward-backward movement (28–45 kHz) creating microbubbles that collapse violently

rationale:
TASS is a sterile, acute anterior segment inflammation developing within 12-24 hours postoperatively caused by toxic
chemical residues on surgical instruments, denatured viscoelastic, or BSS additives.

stem:
What is the management of choice for a large, hard nuclear dropped lens fragment into the mid-vitreous cavity during
cataract surgery?

options.A: Immediate anterior chamber paracentesis and digital massage
options.B: Perform Nd:YAG laser fragmentation of vitreous
options.C: Attempt removal with phaco tip inserted through posterior capsule tear
options.D:
Complete anterior vitrectomy, place IOL (if capsular support permits), close wound, and refer for 3-port Pars Plana Vitrectomy
(PPV) with fragmatome
options.E: Leave fragment and start high-dose topical steroids

rationale:
Surgeons should NEVER chase dropped nuclear fragments into the vitreous from the anterior approach. Secure anterior
segment, perform anterior vitrectomy, close wound, and schedule 3-port PPV with a fragmatome.

stem:
A patient with high myopia undergoing cataract surgery has an axial length of 29.5 mm. What intraoperative complication
risk is significantly elevated during hydrodissection?

options.C: Capsular Block Syndrome and explosive posterior capsule rupture

rationale:
Vigorous hydrodissection in deep capsular bags or posterior polar cataracts can trap fluid behind a large nucleus, causing
Capsular Block Syndrome and sudden posterior capsule blow-out.

stem:
Which systemic medication is most strongly associated with Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS) during cataract
surgery?
rationale:
Tamsulosin causes irreversible relaxation/atrophy of iris dilator smooth muscle cells, leading to the IFIS triad: flaccid iris
stroma, propensity for iris prolapse, and progressive intraoperative miosis.

stem: What is the classic Purkinje-Sanson image finding in an aphakic eye?

options.B: Images 1 and 2 present; Images 3 and 4 absent
options.E: Images 3 and 4 present; Images 1 and 2 absent

rationale:
TASS is a sterile, acute anterior segment inflammation developing within 12-24 hours postoperatively caused by toxic
chemical residues on surgical instruments, denatured viscoelastic, or BSS additives.

stem:
In a infant diagnosed with dense bilateral congenital cataracts at birth, what is the critical therapeutic window for surgery
to prevent irreversible stimulus-deprivation amblyopia?

options.C: Surgery is postponed until teenage years
options.D: Within the first 4 to 6 weeks of life
options.E: At 2 years of age when eye growth stabilizes

rationale:
Visual cortex deprivation amblyopia becomes irreversible if dense bilateral congenital cataracts are not surgically cleared
within the first 4-6 weeks of life (for unilateral cataracts, within 4-8 weeks).

stem: What is the principal optical advantage of a toric intraocular lens (IOL)?

options.A: Corrects pre-existing regular corneal astigmatism by aligning lens steep meridian with corneal steep axis
options.D: Automatically adjusts focal length via ciliary muscle contraction

rationale:
Toric IOLs possess cylinder power ground into specific meridians to neutralize regular corneal astigmatism. Precise rotational
alignment on the steep corneal axis is required.

stem:
A 70-year-old male presents with hypermature cataract and hyperemic eye. IOP is 38 mmHg. Slit lamp reveals heavy
corneal edema, deep AC with circulating white shiny particles, and an intact lens capsule. Diagnosis?
rationale:
Hypermature cataract + intact capsule + leaking heavy protein + macrophage reaction clogging trabecular meshwork =
Phacolytic Glaucoma.

stem: What is the management of choice for Phacomorphic Glaucoma unresponsive to maximal medical therapy?

options.B: Emergency Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) followed by cataract extraction once IOP controlled

rationale:
Immediate medical lowering of IOP and LPI breaks pupillary block, opening the angle temporarily to allow safer definitive
cataract extraction.

stem:
In Goldmann Applanation Tonometer calibration and theory, what specific corneal thickness (pachymetry) is assumed
for standard accurate IOP measurement?
rationale:
Goldmann applanation tonometry (Imbert-Fick law) is calibrated for a central corneal thickness (CCT) of ~520-550 um. Thinner
corneas artificially understate IOP; thicker corneas artificially overstate IOP.

stem:
In the Imbert-Fick law applicable to applanation tonometry, what is the exact diameter of the corneal area applanated by
the Goldmann prism?
rationale:
At an applanated diameter of 3.06 mm, the capillary attraction force of tear film balances the corneal rigidity resistance force,
making area = 7.35 mm2.

stem: Which anatomical structure forms the anterior boundary of the trabecular meshwork visible on Gonioscopy?
rationale:
From anterior to posterior, gonioscopic landmarks are: 1. Schwalbe's line, 2. Trabecular meshwork (non-pigmented then
pigmented), 3. Scleral spur, 4. Ciliary body band.

stem:
In Pigment Dispersion Syndrome, what specific gonioscopic landmark is created by intense pigment deposition anterior
to Schwalbe's line?
rationale:
Sampaolesi line is a distinct line of dark pigment deposited on or anterior to Schwalbe's line, pathognomonic for pigment
dispersion syndrome and pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

stem:
In Pseudoexfoliation Glaucoma (PEX), what is the biochemical nature of the fibrillar material deposited on the anterior
lens capsule and trabecular meshwork?

options.B: Amyloid-like elastic fibrillar basement membrane material

rationale:
PEX is a systemic elastic microfibrillopathy driven by LOXL1 gene variants, producing abnormal fibrillar protein-glycoprotein
complexes deposited throughout anterior segment structures.

stem:
What is the classic visual field defect associated with damage to retinal nerve fibers entering the superior temporal pole
of the optic disc (Bjerrum area)?

options.D: Inferior arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma respecting the horizontal raphe

rationale:
Damage to nerve fiber bundles entering the superior temporal disc pole causes an inferior arcuate scotoma arching from the
blind spot around fixation to terminate at the nasal horizontal raphe.

stem:
Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) selectively targets which subcellular structures in the trabecular meshwork
without thermal destruction of collagen architecture?

options.E: Pigmented trabecular meshwork cells via selective photothermolysis of melanin granules

rationale:
SLT uses a frequency-doubled Q-switched Nd:YAG laser (532 nm) with 3 ns pulse duration targeting melanin pigment in TM
cells without causing thermal damage to structural trabecular framework.

stem:
In Trabeculectomy surgery, what pharmacological intraoperative antimetabolite is applied to the scleral flap bed to inhibit
fibroblast proliferation and prevent bleb scarring?
rationale:
Mitomycin C (alkylating agent) or 5-FU (pyrimidine analog) are applied topically via sponges to inhibit episcleral fibroblast
proliferation and surgical site scarring.

stem: What is the primary clinical manifestation of 'Malignant Glaucoma' (Ciliary Block Glaucoma / Aqueous Misdirection)?

options.A: Massive choroidal detachment with scleral spur avulsion
options.B:
Uniform shallowing or flattening of central and peripheral AC with elevated IOP post-incisional surgery, caused by backward
aqueous flow into vitreous cavity
options.C: Deep AC with IOP of 5 mmHg
options.D: Severe iris bombé with deep central AC
options.E: Spontaneous posterior capsule tear with vitreous prolapse into AC

rationale:
Aqueous misdirection involves backward diversion of aqueous humor into or behind the vitreous body, displacing ciliary
processes and lens/IOL diaphragm anteriorly, flattening the entire AC.

stem: What is the initial medical therapy of choice to break Malignant Glaucoma?

options.A: Cycloplegics (Topical Atropine 1%) + Aqueous suppressants + IV Mannitol
options.C: Bilateral digital ocular massage for 30 minutes

rationale:
Atropine relaxes ciliary muscle, pulling the lens-iris diaphragm backward while tightening zonules; miotics (Pilocarpine) worsen
malignant glaucoma and are strictly contraindicated.

stem: In Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG), what non-IOP risk factors are strongly linked to optic nerve damage?

options.C: Nocturnal systemic hypotension, vasospasm (Raynaud's/migraine), and sleep apnea

rationale:
NTG features glaucomatous neuropathy at normal IOP (<=21 mmHg) driven by vascular dysregulation, nocturnal dipping of
systemic blood pressure, Raynaud's phenomenon, and migraine.

stem:
Which anti-glaucoma medication class is contraindicated in pediatric patients under 2 years of age due to risk of severe
central nervous system depression and apnea?
rationale:
Brimonidine crosses the blood-brain barrier in young children, causing life-threatening CNS depression, somnolence,
bradycardia, hypotension, and respiratory apnea.

stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of Netarsudil in glaucoma treatment?

options.A: Inhibition of Rho-kinase (ROCK) leading to increased trabecular outflow facility and decreased episcleral venous pressure

rationale:
Netarsudil is a Rho-kinase inhibitor that targets trabecular meshwork cellular cytoskeleton to increase outflow facility, while
also reducing episcleral venous pressure.

stem: What is the pathognomonic visual field loss stage termed when only a tiny island of vision remains in terminal glaucoma?

options.A: Temporal island of vision (and/or small central field)

rationale:
End-stage advanced glaucoma spares only the far peripheral temporal island and a tiny central macular field before total light
perception loss.

stem:
In Diabetic Retinopathy, what specific histopathological cell loss represents the earliest microvascular lesion leading to
capillary acellularity and microaneurysm formation?

options.A: Loss of retinal pigment epithelial cells
options.C: Loss of internal limiting membrane astrocytes
options.D: Selective loss of intramural Pericytes (1:1 pericyte-to-endothelial cell ratio lost)

rationale:
Hyperglycemia-induced sorbitol accumulation leads to selective apoptosis of capillary pericytes, weakening vessel walls and
causing microaneurysms and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier.

stem:
What constitutes the defining criteria for 'Clinically Significant Macular Edema' (CSME) under original ETDRS
guidelines?

options.A:
Retinal thickening at or within 500 microns of foveal center, OR hard exudates at/within 500 microns with adjacent thickening,
OR retinal thickening >= 1 disc area in size within 1 disc diameter of foveal center
options.C: Presence of cotton wool spots in 4 quadrants
options.D: Neovascularization of optic disc > 1/3 disc area
options.E: Vitreous hemorrhage with tractional retinal detachment

rationale:
ETDRS defined CSME based on biomicroscopic findings of thickening/exudates involving or threatening the foveal center,
dictating focal/grid laser treatment.

stem: What is the defining criteria for 'Very Severe Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy' (Severe NPDR 4-2-1 rule)?

options.A: Hard exudates forming a complete star at fovea
options.E:
Presence of 2 or more criteria of the 4-2-1 rule (Microaneurysms in 4 quadrants, Venous beading in 2+ quadrants, IRMA in 1+
quadrant)

rationale: Severe NPDR meets 1 criterion of the 4-2-1 rule; Very Severe NPDR meets 2 or more criteria without overt neovascularization.

stem:
In Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), what anatomical zone classification corresponds to the optic disc-centered circle
with a radius twice the distance from disc to fovea?
rationale:
Zone I is the innermost zone centered on the optic disc, extending from disc to twice the disc-fovea distance (highest risk
zone).

stem: In ROP, what specific clinical finding defines 'Plus Disease'?

options.E: Significant arterial tortuosity and venous dilation in the posterior retinal pole

rationale:
Plus disease indicates severe active ischemia characterized by marked dilation and tortuosity of posterior retinal arterioles and
venules.

stem:
A 65-year-old high myope presents with sudden onset flashes of light (photopsia) and showers of floaters.
Biomicroscopy reveals pigment granules in the anterior vitreous ('tobacco dust' / Shaffer's sign). What underlying pathology
does this pathognomonic sign indicate?

options.B: Full-thickness retinal tear / break (precursor to Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment)

rationale:
Shaffer's sign (tobacco dust) represents liberated RPE cells floating in the anterior vitreous following a full-thickness retinal
break, highly predictive of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

stem: What is the fundamental pathogenetic mechanism of Exudative (Serous) Retinal Detachment?

options.A: Primary atrophy of optic nerve fibers
options.B: Full-thickness retinal tear allowing fluid vitreous to enter subretinal space
options.C: Vitreoretinal fibrovascular membranes pulling sensory retina off RPE
options.E: Breakdown of inner or outer blood-retinal barrier leading to fluid accumulation in subretinal space without retinal break

rationale:
Exudative RD results from subretinal fluid accumulation secondary to RPE/choroidal pathology (e.g., VKH syndrome, choroidal
tumor, toxemia of pregnancy) without a retinal tear or vitreous traction.

stem:
In Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), what is the histological composition of Drusen deposited between the
basal lamina of the RPE and the inner collagenous layer of Bruch's membrane?

options.D: Lipofuscin, apolipoproteins, complement factors (C3, C5, Factor H), and cellular debris

rationale:
Drusen consist of metabolic waste products from uncycled photoreceptor outer segments, including lipofuscin, apolipoprotein
E, complement components (C3, C5, Factor H), and inflammatory debris.

stem:
What is the primary molecular target of Intravitreal Aflibercept (Eylea) used in Neovascular AMD and Diabetic Macular
Edema?

options.B: Recombinant monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A only
options.C: Fusion protein acting as a soluble decoy receptor binding VEGF-A, VEGF-B, and Placental Growth Factor (PlGF)

rationale:
Aflibercept is a recombinant fusion decoy receptor protein that binds all isoforms of VEGF-A, VEGF-B, and PlGF with higher
affinity than native receptors.

stem: What is the pathognomonic fluorescein angiographic (FFA) pattern seen in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR)?

options.C: 'Smoke-stack' or 'expanding dot' hyperfluorescence leaking into subretinal space

rationale:
CSCR typically displays an expanding focal point of leakage from the RPE into the subretinal space, rising vertically and
spreading like a 'smoke-stack' or umbrella.

stem: In Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP), what is the classic triad of fundoscopic findings?

options.A: Flame hemorrhages, Roth spots, and cotton wool spots
options.B: Bone-spicule intraretinal pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation, and waxy pallor of optic disc
options.C: Cherry-red spot, box-carring, and retinal pallor
options.D: Angioid streaks, drusen, and disciform scar
options.E: Hard exudates, microaneurysms, and macular edema

rationale:
RP hallmark triad: 1. Perivascular bone-spicule pigment deposits in mid-periphery, 2. Marked retinal arteriolar attenuation, 3.
Waxy disc pallor.

stem: What electroretinogram (ERG) component wave is selectively abolished early in Retinitis Pigmentosa?
rationale:
RP primary affects rod photoreceptors first, causing night blindness (nyctalopia) and early severe reduction/extinction of
scotopic ERG waves.

stem:
A 20-year-old patient presents with bilateral reduced vision. Electro-oculogram (EOG) shows a severely depressed
Arden ratio (<1.5), while standard ERG is completely normal. Fundus shows a yellow egg-yolk (vitelliform) lesion at the
macula. What gene is mutated?

options.A: BEST1 gene encoding Bestrophin-1 (Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy)

rationale:
Best disease (autosomal dominant) is caused by BEST1 mutation, featuring an abnormal EOG (Arden ratio <1.5) with normal
ERG, displaying a vitelliform macular lesion.

stem: What is the fundamental defect in Stargardt Disease (Juvenile Macular Degeneration)?

options.C: Autosomal recessive mutation in ABCA4 gene leading to toxic accumulation of A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) in RPE

rationale:
ABCA4 gene mutations impair N-retinylidene-PE transport out of photoreceptor outer segments, leading to bis-retinoid A2E
accumulation in RPE cells, causing 'dark choroid' on FFA.

stem:
In Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment, what surgical procedure places a silicone element scleral buckle around the
globe exterior?

options.A: Indents sclera inward towards detached retina to relieve vitreoretinal traction over retinal break
options.B: Destroys ciliary epithelium to reduce IOP
options.C: Pushes retina outward against orbital wall
options.D: Replaces vitreous gel completely with silicone oil

rationale:
Scleral buckling indents the eyewall inward toward the retinal tear, reapposing RPE to neurosensory retina and relieving
vitreous traction.

stem:
What intraocular gas tamponade agent has the longest longevity (~6 to 8 weeks) inside the eye following Pars Plana
Vitrectomy?
rationale: C3F8 gas expands to ~4x its initial volume and persists inside the vitreous cavity for 6-8 weeks; SF6 lasts 10-14 days.

stem:
What is the pathognomonic histological hallmark of Sympathetic Ophthalmitis developing in the non-injured
'sympathizing' eye following penetrating ocular trauma to the 'exciting' eye?

options.B: Acute necrotizing polymorphonuclear infiltrate of retina
options.E:
Non-necrotizing granulomatous panuveitis with Dalen-Fuchs nodules (epithelioid cells between RPE and Bruch's membrane)
sparing the choriocapillaris

rationale:
Sympathetic Ophthalmitis is an autoimmune T-cell mediated response against ocular self-antigens (retinal S-antigen /
interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein), featuring Dalen-Fuchs nodules and diffuse granulomatous uveal thickening sparing
choriocapillaris.

stem:
In Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) Syndrome, what systemic non-ocular manifestations accompany the bilateral exudative
retinal detachments during the convalescent stage?

options.E: Poliosis, vitiligo, alopecia, dysacusis (sensorineural hearing loss), and meningismus

rationale:
VKH is a systemic autoimmune disease targeting melanocytes, causing bilateral granulomatous panuveitis, exudative RD,
poliosis (whitening of lashes), vitiligo, alopecia, acoustic disturbances, and meningismus.

stem: What is the classic triad of Behçet's Disease affecting the eye?

options.A: Interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness, and Hutchinson teeth
options.B: Uveitis, parotiditis, and facial nerve palsy
options.C: Recurrent occlusive necrotizing retinal vasculitis, shifting hypopyon iridocyclitis, and systemic aphthous mucosal ulcerations
options.E: Rheumatoid arthritis, dry eye, and scleritis

rationale:
Behçet's disease is an HLA-B51 linked systemic occlusive vasculitis characterized by recurrent non-granulomatous uveitis with
transient mobile hypopyon and severe necrotizing retinal vasculitis.

stem:
In Fuchs' Heterochromic Iridocyclitis (FHI), what key clinical feature differentiates it from most other forms of anterior
uveitis?

options.A:
ABSENCE of posterior synechiae despite chronic low-grade AC inflammation, accompanied by diffuse stellate KPs, iris
atrophy/heterochromia, and early cataract/glaucoma
options.B: Presence of dense Koeppe nodules in 100% of cases
options.D: Presence of large mutton-fat KPs restricted to inferior cornea
options.E: Presence of severe pain and heavy fibrin formation

rationale:
Fuchs' Uveitis Syndrome is characterized by iris heterochromia, small diffuse stellate keratic precipitates distributed across
entire endothelium, absence of posterior synechiae, and steroid resistance.

stem:
What is the definitive initial diagnostic test of choice when Sarcoidosis is suspected in a patient with bilateral
granulomatous panuveitis and candle-wax drippings (taches de bougie) retinal vasculitis?

options.D: Serum Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) level & High-Resolution Chest CT (HRCT)

rationale:
Sarcoidosis produces non-caseating granulomas. Diagnostic confirmation relies on elevated serum ACE, serum lysozyme,
and chest CT demonstrating bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

stem:
What pathogen causes 'Neuroretinitis' characterized by optic disc edema accompanied by a macular star of hard
exudates?
rationale:
Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) is the classic cause of neuroretinitis: optic disc swelling + fluid exuding into outer
plexiform layer forming a 360-degree star of hard exudates at Henle's layer.

stem: What is the classic fundus appearance of active Toxoplasma Retinochoroiditis?

options.C: Multiple creamy white spots in deep choroid
options.D:
Focal, white-yellow necrotizing retinochoroiditis adjacent to an old hyperpigmented scar with intense overlying vitreous haze
('headlight in the fog')

rationale:
Reactivation of congenital/acquired Toxoplasma cysts produces satellite focal retinitis adjacent to a pigmented scar, shrouded
by dense vitreous inflammation ('headlight in the fog').

stem:
In Trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, Ba, C), what specific cicatricial tarsal conjunctival sign represents
the WHO 'TS' stage?

options.E: Arlt's line (linear white scar parallel to superior tarsal margin)

rationale:
WHO Trachoma grading: TF (Follicular), TI (Intense inflammation), TS (Trachomatous scarring - Arlt's line), TT (Trichiasis),
CO (Corneal opacity).

stem: What anatomical structure degenerates to form Herbert's Pits in late Trachoma?

options.B: Limbal follicles undergoing necrosis and cicatrization, leaving cup-like depressions

rationale:
Resolution and scarring of active lymphoid follicles located at the corneal limbus leave permanent shallow cup-like row of clear
depressions termed Herbert's pits.

stem:
In Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), what specific cellular infiltrates compose 'Horner-Trantas Dots' located at the
limbus?

options.A: Clumped Eosinophils and epithelial cell debris

rationale:
Horner-Trantas dots are gel-like white elevated spots at the limbus in limbal/mixed VKC, composed of necrotic eosinophil
aggregates and epithelial debris.

stem: What is the drug of choice for oral mass drug administration (SAFE strategy) to treat endemic Trachoma?

options.E: Single dose Oral Azithromycin (20 mg/kg up to 1g)

rationale:
The 'A' in the WHO SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement) stands for mass
treatment with single-dose oral Azithromycin (or topical Erythromycin).

stem:
A 7-day-old neonate presents with purulent conjunctivitis. Giemsa staining of conjunctival scrapings reveals basophilic
Intracytoplasmic Inclusion Bodies within epithelial cells. What is the diagnosis?

options.C: Chemical conjunctivitis secondary to silver nitrate

rationale:
Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum presents between 5-14 days post-birth; Giemsa stain demonstrating
Halberstaedter-Prowazek intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies confirms Chlamydia.

stem:
What systemic complication must be monitored and treated when systemic Erythromycin or Azithromycin is
administered for Chlamydial Ophthalmia Neonatorum?
rationale:
Oral Erythromycin/Azithromycin in infants under 6 weeks carries a known risk of Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis,
requiring parental counseling regarding vomiting.

stem:
Parinaud Oculoglandular Syndrome is characterized by unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis accompanied by severe
ipsilateral preauricular/submandibular lymphadenopathy. What is the most common etiology?
rationale:
Bartonella henselae inoculation via cat scratch/flea contact onto conjunctiva is the primary cause of Parinaud oculoglandular
syndrome.

stem:
A patient presents with a visual field defect showing incongruous homonymous hemianopia with associated Relative
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) in the eye contralateral to the lesion. Where is the lesion located?
rationale:
Optic tract lesions carry fibers from both eyes prior to synapse in LGN, producing an INCONGRUOUS homonymous
hemianopia and a contralateral RAPD (because tract contains more nasal fibers from contralateral eye).

stem:
A lesion located in 'Meyer's loop' passing through the Temporal Lobe causes what characteristic quadrant visual field
defect?

options.B: Inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')
options.E: Superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')

rationale:
Temporal lobe lesions disrupt inferior optic radiation fibers (Meyer's loop) sweeping around temporal horn of lateral ventricle,
causing contralateral Superior Homonymous Quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

stem: Parietal lobe lesions damaging the superior optic radiations produce what specific visual field defect?

options.E: Inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')

rationale:
Parietal lobe lesions damage superior optic radiation fibers passing directly through parietal cortex to calcarine fissure, causing
Inferior Homonymous Quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor').

stem:
In Occipital Cortex infarction due to Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) occlusion, what specific macular phenomenon is
classically demonstrated on perimetry?

options.B: Macular Sparing (preservation of central 3 to 5 degrees of visual field due to dual blood supply from Middle Cerebral Artery)
options.D: Macular involvement with total central loss

rationale:
Occipital pole representing the fovea has dual vascular supply from PCA and MCA branches. PCA occlusion causes
homonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARING.

stem: What is the light-near pupillary dissociation mechanism in Argyll Robertson Pupil?

options.A: Paradoxical pupillary dilation in bright light
options.B: Bilateral small miotic irregular pupils that respond to Light but NOT to Accommodation
options.C: Unilateral dilated pupil responding slowly to light
options.D: Bilateral small miotic irregular pupils that respond to Accommodation/Near reflex but DO NOT respond to Light stimulus
options.E: Total fixed dilated pupils unresponsive to light or near

rationale:
Argyll Robertson pupil (classic in neurosyphilis/tabes dorsalis) features bilateral small, irregular pupils that Accommodate but
Do Not React to Light (Light-Near Dissociation).

stem:
In Adie's Tonic Pupil, what low-concentration topical parasympathomimetic drop causes hypersensitive pupillary
constriction due to denervation supersensitivity?
rationale:
Postganglionic ciliary ganglion denervation in Adie's pupil induces cholinergic receptor upregulation. Dilute Pilocarpine
(0.125%), which does not constrict a normal pupil, produces marked constriction in Adie's tonic pupil.

stem:
A 45-year-old female presents with severe dry eye and exposure keratitis following complete facial nerve (CN VII)
paralysis. What surgical procedure permanently or temporarily fuses the upper and lower eyelid margins to protect the
cornea?
rationale:
Tarsorrhaphy is the surgical suturing together of the upper and lower eyelids (partially or completely) to narrow the palpebral
fissure and protect the cornea in lagophthalmos/exposure keratitis.

stem:
In evaluating a child with Congenital Ptosis, what specific quantitative measurement determines whether a Levator
Resection vs. Frontalis Sling procedure is indicated?

options.C:
Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS) function / excursion (mm of lid movement from downgaze to upgaze with frontalis muscle
blocked)

rationale:
LPS function dictates surgical choice: Good function (>8 mm) -> Fasanella-Servat or LPS resection; Fair function (5-7 mm) ->
LPS resection; Poor function (<4 mm) -> Frontalis sling.

stem:
Fasanella-Servat procedure is indicated for mild ptosis (1-2 mm) with good LPS function (>10 mm). What anatomical
structures are excision-resected during this internal approach?

options.E: Tarsal plate superior border, Müller's muscle, and overlying palpebral conjunctiva

rationale: Fasanella-Servat is a posterior approach resecting a strip of superior tarsus, Müller's muscle, and conjunctiva.

stem: What clinical test differentiates Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Synkinesis from isolated congenital ptosis?

options.D: Retraction or elevation of the ptotic lid upon movement of the jaw (chewing, suction, or lateral pterygoid movement)

rationale:
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a congenital misdirection where CN V3 (motor to external pterygoid) abnormally
innervates the ipsilateral levator palpebrae (CN III).

stem:
In Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO), what specific embryonic membranous structure fails to canalize
at the inferior meatus of the nose?
rationale:
Imperforate membrane at the Valve of Hasner (distal end of nasolacrimal duct at inferior nasal meatus) causes >90% of
CNLDO cases.

stem:
If Crigler digital lacrimal massage and topical antibiotics fail to resolve CNLDO by 12 months of age, what is the next
sequential surgical intervention?

options.A: Intubation with silicone tube for 2 years
options.C: Nasolacrimal Duct Probing under general anesthesia

rationale:
Initial probing with a Bowman probe through the punctum and lacrimal system to rupture the membrane at the Valve of Hasner
achieves >90% success between 12-18 months.

stem:
What anatomical bony landmark is created during Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery to bypass an obstructed
nasolacrimal duct?

options.E: Osteotomy through the lacrimal bone and frontal process of maxilla connecting lacrimal sac directly to middle nasal meatus

rationale:
DCR creates a bony ostium between the lacrimal fossa (lacrimal bone + frontal process of maxilla) and middle nasal meatus,
anastomosing lacrimal sac mucosal flaps to nasal mucosal flaps.

stem:
Alkali chemical injuries (e.g., ammonia, quicklime/calcium hydroxide) are far more devastating to the eye than acid
burns. What is the fundamental chemical mechanism driving alkali tissue destruction?

options.A: Liquefactive necrosis breaking down cell membranes and saponifying fatty acids, allowing rapid deep penetration into AC
options.D: Coagulative necrosis forming a protective barrier that limits deep penetration

rationale:
Alkali agents saponify cell membrane lipids and denature proteoglycans, causing liquefactive necrosis that penetrates rapidly
into the anterior chamber within minutes. Acids cause coagulative necrosis which limits penetration.

stem:
What clinical sign on slit-lamp examination indicates severe limbal ischemia and poor visual prognosis following a severe
chemical burn?

options.A: Limbal blanching (porcelain white avascular appearance of limbal conjunctiva and episclera)

rationale:
Roper-Hall classification grades chemical burns based on corneal clarity and limbal ischemia. Limbal blanching (porcelain
white) indicates destruction of limbal stem cells and avascular necrosis.

stem:
In an Orbital Blow-Out Fracture involving the maxillary floor, what extraocular muscle entrapment causes double vision
(diplopia) on upward gaze?

options.A: Inferior rectus muscle and/or Inferior oblique muscle / orbital fat herniation into maxillary sinus

rationale:
Fracture of thin orbital floor (maxillary bone) leads to herniation of orbital fat and entrapment of the inferior rectus / inferior
oblique muscle complex, restricting upward movement.

stem:
What type of refractive error exists when parallel rays of light coming from infinity enter the unaccommodated eye and
focus at TWO separate focal lines at right angles to each other?
rationale:
Astigmatism occurs when unequal curvature along different corneal/lens meridians creates two focal lines separated by an
focal interval (Conoid of Sturm).

stem:
What optical phenomenon occurs when an aphakic patient is fitted with high-plus spectacle lenses (+10.0 D), causing a
ring-shaped scotoma in the peripheral field?

options.A: 'Jack-in-the-box' phenomenon (prismatic effect producing a circular motion scotoma)

rationale:
High plus spectacle lenses act as strong base-in prisms at the periphery, creating a ring scotoma. Objects entering and exiting
this scotoma pop in and out ('Jack-in-the-box' phenomenon).

stem: In Accommodative Esotropia, what is the underlying refractive state of the eye and the mechanism of strabismus?

options.A: Uncorrected Hypermetropia causing excessive ciliary accommodation coupled with excessive convergence (High AC/A ratio)

rationale:
Uncorrected hypermetropia forces continuous accommodation to clear blurred vision. Excess accommodation drives
synkinetic accommodative convergence, causing esotropia.

stem: What extraocular muscle is primarily tested when asking a patient to look INWARD (adduct) and then DOWNWARD?
rationale:
The Superior Oblique muscle intorts, abducts, and depresses. When the eye is adducted 39 degrees, its optical axis aligns
with the muscle pull, making it a pure depressor.

stem: What specific cranial nerve palsy causes a head tilt toward the CONTRALATERAL shoulder to compensate for diplopia?

options.B: 4th nerve palsy (Trochlear nerve innervating Superior Oblique)

rationale:
Trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy causes extorsion and hyperdeviation. Patients tilt head toward the OPPOSITE (contralateral)
shoulder to compensate and eliminate vertical/torsional diplopia.

stem: What is the most common primary intraocular malignant tumor of childhood?
rationale:
Retinoblastoma (RB1 gene mutation on chromosome 13q14) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in infants
and young children.

stem:
What pathognomonic rosette structure composed of tumor cells surrounding a central lumen containing cytoplasmic
extensions is characteristic of Retinoblastoma on histology?
rationale:
Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (specific for photoreceptor differentiation in retinoblastoma) feature columnar cells surrounding
a clear central lumen containing microvilli.

stem:
In Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Orbitopathy), what specific glycosaminoglycan accumulation and lymphocytic
infiltration cause extraocular muscle enlargement?

options.B: Deposition of calcium phosphate in muscle sheaths
options.D: Hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate deposition within extraocular muscle bellies (sparing tendons)
options.E: Amyloid plaque deposition in muscle tendons

rationale:
TSH receptor autoantibodies activate orbital fibroblasts to produce hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid), causing
marked edema and swelling of muscle bellies while sparing tendons.

stem:
Which extraocular muscle is most frequently and severely involved in Thyroid Eye Disease, leading to restrictive
hypotropia and diplopia on vertical gaze?
rationale:
Order of muscle involvement in TED (Mnemonic: IMSLO) = Inferior rectus > Medial rectus > Superior rectus > Lateral rectus >
Obliques. Inferior rectus fibrosis restricts elevation.

stem: In Ocular Embryology, which ocular structures originate from NEURAL CREST CELLS?

options.C: Corneal stroma, Corneal endothelium, Sclera, Trabecular meshwork, Ciliary muscle, and Iris stroma

rationale:
Neural crest cells give rise to corneal stroma & endothelium, sclera, trabecular meshwork, ciliary body stroma & muscle, iris
stroma, and orbital cartilage/bone. Neural ectoderm forms retina, RPE, optic nerve, iris pigment epithelium, and ciliary epithelium.
